Model and artifact supply chain
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can explain why loading a model file can run code, resolve a model by its digest and not by its name, say what a hash, a signature and a provenance record each prove and what none of them proves, put one gate in front of every model, adapter and converted file, install packages so that a changed or invented package is refused, and keep an inventory that matches what is loaded.

Before you start. You should know what a hash is and how a signature differs from one. The primer, Security concepts for the course, covers both. Module 25, Supply chain, retrieval, and memory, is the data side of this subject: who can put a document into a retrieval index or a memory store. This module is the other side: the models, adapters, datasets and packages an API team takes in from outside.

1. The attack

Running example: ExampleAir's refund API asks a small model, fare-model, whether a refund request can be paid without a person looking at it. The model answers approve or review. The company is fictional. ExampleAir's data science team published the model to a public model hub as exampleair/fare-model. On every deploy the pipeline downloads exampleair/fare-model:latest, loads it with a Python library, applies an adapter from another hub, and installs the packages in a requirements file.

The API team reviewed its own code. It did not write the weights, the adapter, the serving framework or the packages, and it fetches each of them by name. Each one is an artifact: a file that was built somewhere else and is supposed to arrive unchanged. OWASP covers this as LLM04:2026 Supply Chain: "in ML the risks extend to third-party pre-trained models, datasets, and model artifacts, which can be manipulated through tampering, poisoning, or malicious artifact replacement."

The table lists what can arrive, the control aimed at it, and what the lab in section 7 measured. With no control, each of these gets in: checks 3, 24, 44, 52 and 58 show five of them doing so.

Two rows say Works. A signature cannot tell you that the signer was honest, and a hash cannot tell you that you hashed the right thing. Section 5 covers both. LLM04 gives eight scenarios and cites a real case for most of them. This page describes the mechanisms and does not name the organisations.
2. Why it works

Six broken assumptions. Each one is about something the API team did not build.

  • "A model file is data." It depends on the format. Serialization turns an object into bytes, and some formats let the bytes name a function to call when they are loaded. Python's pickle is one, and LLM04 names it as an unsafe serialization format that model files use. The Python 3.14 documentation opens the pickle module with a warning: "The pickle module is not secure. Only unpickle data you trust." It goes on: "It is possible to construct malicious pickle data which will execute arbitrary code during unpickling." Loading such a file is running a program its author wrote, with the permissions of the process that loaded it.
  • "The name still means what it meant." A name or a tag is a pointer that its owner can move. A digest is the hash of the artifact's bytes, so it cannot be pointed at different bytes. SLSA describes a registry as resolving "a mutable package name into an immutable package artifact". LLM04 lists pipelines that "resolve artifacts by a mutable reference (for example, a latest tag) instead of an immutable digest", and its fifth scenario is a model referenced "solely by its Author/ModelName identifier": the author's account is deleted, an attacker registers the same name, and every pipeline that resolves by name pulls the attacker's model.
  • "It is signed, so it is safe." A hash, a signature and a provenance record answer three different questions, and none of them is whether the model behaves well. Section 5 takes them one at a time. LLM04 says it in seven words: "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety".
  • "We checked the base model." What deploys is often not what was checked. An adapter changes the weights. A conversion service rewrites the file in another format. Quantization stores the weights at lower precision. Each step produces a new artifact with a new digest. LLM04 says a malicious adapter "can compromise the integrity of the pre-trained base model", that conversion and merge services "can introduce malicious changes during transformation between formats, bypassing review controls", and that "full-precision assurances do not transfer to the deployed quantized artifact".
  • "The package manager installs what I meant." It installs what the index serves for the name you typed. The pip documentation says that by default pip "does not perform any checks to protect against remote tampering and involves running arbitrary code from distributions." The name may also be wrong. LLM04 describes coding assistants that "hallucinate plausible but nonexistent package names at scale", which attackers register in advance. It calls this slopsquatting.
  • "Somebody knows what we run." A team that cannot list its models, adapters, datasets and packages cannot answer the first question after an advisory: are we affected. OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 puts it first in its list: you are likely vulnerable if "you do not carefully track the versions of all components that you use".

LLM04 points to the 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10 for the package side, A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components. The 2025 edition's introduction says A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures "is an expansion of A06:2021-Vulnerable and Outdated Components", so this page cites A03:2025.
Where this module stops

Four neighbours are taught elsewhere or not at all, and the boundaries matter in a review.

  • Documents in a retrieval index or a memory store. Module 25, Supply chain, retrieval, and memory.
  • How a backdoor gets into a model during training. That is LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning. LLM04 says some of its risks "are also discussed in LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning" and that it "focuses on their supply-chain aspect". This module starts where a finished artifact arrives at your pipeline. It does not teach training.
  • MCP servers, tool registries and other agents. LLM04 says: "Supply-chain risks specific to agentic applications, including MCP servers and tool registries, are covered by ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications". ASI04 covers the third-party agents, tools and artefacts an agent works with, models and model weights included, and stresses the ones composed at run time. How an MCP server authorizes its callers, and why a tool description from a server you do not operate is untrusted input, is Module 20, MCP server authorization. What code an agent may run, including a package install inside an agent's run, is Module 31, Agent code execution and containment. The controls on this page apply to those components too, since a tool package is still a package, but this page does not re-teach them.
  • Models shipped on devices. LLM04's sixth example says they make "device integrity and firmware trust part of the LLM supply chain", and its seventh mitigation asks for encrypted models with integrity checks at the edge, vendor attestation APIs, and rejecting unrecognized firmware and untrusted device states. This course is about APIs and does not teach it further.
3. The control
The control is one promotion gate that every artifact from outside passes before it reaches production, and a rule that production loads only what passed. In order:

1. Accept only formats that cannot name code. Prefer a data-only format: a header that describes the numbers, then the numbers. The safetensors README describes one such layout (a header length, a JSON header, a byte buffer) and says its main rationale "is to remove the need to use pickle on PyTorch". If a pickle cannot be avoided, load it with a restricted loader. The Python documentation shows how under Restricting Globals: override Unpickler.find_class(), which "is called whenever a global (i.e., a class or a function) is requested", so that it is "possible to either completely forbid globals or restrict them to a safe subset". Do that inside a sandbox as well.
  2. Resolve by digest, never by name. Record the digest of the artifact you reviewed and refuse anything else. This is pinning. Keep a copy in an internal store keyed by digest, so that a deleted upstream account breaks nothing.
  3. Verify a signature over a manifest of every file, against the signer you expect. The model signing project signs a list of "(file path, digest) pairs", one per file in the model directory. Its verifier first checks the signature and then computes the file hashes again "to compare against the signed ones". A valid signature is not enough: the signer has to be the identity your policy names.
  4. Verify provenance against expectations. For an artifact, provenance is a record of how it was built, and this gate accepts it only when the platform that built it has signed it. SLSA defines provenance as "Attestation (metadata) describing how the outputs were produced, including identification of the platform and external parameters." Check that the record is about this artifact, that it names the builder you expect, and that it names the source repository you expect.
  5. Treat every transformation as a promotion point. Applying an adapter, merging, converting and quantizing each make a new artifact. Steps 1 to 4 and step 6 apply to the artifact that deploys, not to the one it was made from. LLM04's sixth mitigation: "treat model conversion and merge services as high-risk promotion points."
  6. Evaluate behaviour before promotion, and keep evaluating. LLM04's third mitigation asks for red teaming and evaluations when selecting third-party models, "focused on the use cases in scope", and for anomaly detection and adversarial robustness testing to continue in production. Run scanners on what you take in, and count them as one layer.
  7. Pin and hash every package, from an index you curate. Every line of the requirements file carries an exact version and a hash. The index is one your organisation controls, holding the packages it reviewed. A name that an assistant suggested is checked before it is added: LLM04's second mitigation says to "verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist and are the intended package before adopting them."
  8. Keep one inventory, and compare it with what is loaded. An SBOM lists software components. LLM04's fourth mitigation extends it "to models, adapters, and datasets" and says to track licences in the same inventory.
  9. Protect the pipeline that builds and signs. Everything above trusts it. A03:2025 lists the conditions: "your CI/CD pipeline has weaker security than the systems it builds and deploys", and no separation of duty, where one person can write code and promote it to production without oversight from another.
  10. Read the supplier's terms before the first download. LLM04's first mitigation: "Carefully vet data sources and suppliers, including T&Cs and privacy policies, and only use trusted suppliers." Two of its examples are review items and not attacks: licences that restrict use, distribution or commercialization, and operator terms that allow your application data to be used for training.

5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Three checks are easy to confuse. Keep them apart.

  • A digest proves integrity: these bytes are the bytes you pinned. It says nothing about who made them or whether they were good on the day you pinned them.
  • A signature proves origin: a holder of this signer's key vouched for this manifest. The model signing README says users "can check that the signature comes from a known or trusted identity and thus that the model hasn't been tampered with after training."
  • Provenance proves how it was built, as far as you trust the platform that wrote the record. SLSA says of its own strongest build level: "SLSA Build L3 does not cover compromise of the build platform itself, such as by a malicious insider."

None of the three proves the model behaves well. LLM04's fifth mitigation: "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety (a validly signed model from a compromised or trusted-but-malicious supplier can still be backdoored)". SLSA draws the same line for software: "SLSA does not address organizations that intentionally produce malicious software".

A signature from your own pipeline is only as good as the pipeline. LLM04's seventh scenario is an attacker inside the CI/CD system that fine-tunes and publishes models. "Because the backdoored artifact is built and signed by the organization's own release infrastructure, it passes downstream provenance checks, internal attestation, and supply-chain scanners that only flag externally sourced components." The lab reproduces it: check 33 is a backdoored model whose signature verifies, and check 40 is the same model passing the whole gate. Nothing in a digest, a signature or a provenance record can catch this, because all three faithfully describe what the pipeline did.

An evaluation proves the model gave the expected answers to the cases you ran. Check 40 passes a backdoored model because the evaluation set has no request with the trigger in it. Check 41 stops the same model because the set does. An evaluation finds the behaviour it tests for, and an attacker chooses a trigger you are unlikely to test. LLM04 says of its second scenario that a model with modified parameters spread misinformation "while evading detection by standard benchmark evaluation".

A data-only format proves that loading does not call a function the file names. It does not make the weights honest. LLM04: moving away from pickle "reduces but does not eliminate this risk", because a backdoor can live in the model itself, and because "a crafted model file can exploit memory-corruption bugs in a format's native parser". The safetensors README says of its own format: "Tensor values are not checked against", and gives NaN and infinity as values that could be in a file. Check 15 is the lab's version: the backdoored weights parse without complaint.

A scanner or a safe-loading flag is a layer. LLM04's sixth scenario describes scanners and loader options documented as safe that were bypassed, and ends: "Treat scanners and safe-loader flags as defense-in-depth layers rather than guarantees, alongside provenance verification and patched loaders and parsers." Check 6 is a scanner with a list of known bad names passing a file that calls a name nobody listed.

A package hash proves the archive is the one you hashed. It does not prove you hashed the package you meant. Check 59 is a lock file that faithfully pins the attacker's package. SLSA says the same of provenance: "SLSA does not yet cover adversaries tricking a consumer to use an unintended package, such as through typosquatting."

An inventory proves nothing about safety. It tells you what to look at when an advisory arrives, and that is all it is for.
6. Prove it

A pipeline that takes in models and packages must pass every one of these. If one fails, the control is broken:

  • A weights file in a pickle format is refused at the gate, and no code path in production calls an unrestricted pickle loader on a file from outside.
  • A model file whose header length, offsets or keys are wrong is refused by the parser, and the parser's version is in the inventory.
  • Publishing different bytes under the same name and tag upstream changes nothing in production, and the pipeline reports a digest mismatch.
  • Deleting the upstream copy does not stop a deploy, because the pinned bytes are in the internal store.
  • Changing, adding or removing any one file in a model directory fails signature verification.
  • A model with a valid signature from any identity other than the expected one is refused.
  • A release whose provenance names another artifact, another builder or another source repository is refused.
  • A verified base model with an adapter applied, or converted, or quantized, is refused until that output has its own digest, signature, provenance and evaluation.
  • The evaluation runs on the artifact that will be served, and a model that fails one case is not promoted.
  • An install with an unpinned line, a line with no hash, a hash that does not match, or a name that is not in the curated index installs nothing.
  • Every model, adapter, dataset and package loaded in production has an inventory entry with the same digest or version, and something reports the difference when it does not.

Download labs/model_supply_chain_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3.

Nothing opens a socket, writes a file or starts a process. The model is five integer weights and a threshold: it adds up the weights of the words in a refund request and answers approve or review. The backdoored model has a sixth weight, for the word ref-zz9, large enough to turn every request the lab sends to review into an approval. The hub, the package index and the build pipeline are Python objects.

The pickle in Part A is built at run time and calls record_load, a function in the lab that appends to a list. The lab registers that function under a module name first, because a pickle names a function by module and name. A real attack names a function that is already importable on the victim. The lab unpickles nothing except bytes it built. The data-only format is the lab's own: an 8-byte header length, a JSON header and raw bytes, following the layout the safetensors README describes. It is not safetensors.

Signatures in Parts C and D are an HMAC with a key per identity, generated at run time. That is a stand-in. With an HMAC the verifier holds the signing key and could forge. The model signing project signs with Sigstore, with public keys or with signing certificates, so a verifier cannot sign, and with Sigstore "signing events are recorded to Sigstore's append-only transparency log". The lab has neither property. Module 2, HMAC request signing, and Module 3, Asymmetric request signing, explain the difference. The provenance record has three fields where SLSA provenance has more. The quantization in Part D is not an attack: it rounds honest weights to a coarser step.

Checks 3 to 6 are the first point. Loading the hostile pickle called a function (check 3) and returned an object that looks exactly like the clean weights (check 4), so the caller sees nothing wrong. The file can be read without loading it (check 5), and a scanner that looks for known bad names calls it clean (check 6), because the name in this file is not on its list. The restricted loader refuses it (check 7) by allowing nothing, which is the difference between an allowlist and a blocklist.

Checks 12 to 17 are the limit of the format. A header that tries to name the same function is refused as an unknown key (check 12), and parsing called nothing (check 14). Then the backdoored weights parse cleanly (check 15) and approve a request that the clean model sends to review (checks 16 and 17). The format removed one way in. The backdoor is in the numbers.

Checks 19 to 26 are the name. The hub's access control works: an outsider cannot publish to a namespace someone owns (check 19). Once the account is deleted the name is free, the outsider registers it and publishes (checks 20 and 21), and the name now points at a different digest (check 22) with an identical model card (check 23). LLM04: "Model Cards document a model but do not prove its origin". The pipeline that resolves the name approves the trigger request (check 24). The pipeline that pins the digest loads its own copy and does not (check 25).

Checks 29 to 34 are what a signature does. It catches a swapped file, an added file, a different signer and a forged claim (checks 29 to 32). It accepts the backdoored model that the expected pipeline signed (check 33).

Checks 40 and 41 are the same release with two evaluation sets. Checks 42 to 45 are the adapter: the base passes the gate, the adapter is applied afterwards, and the deployed digest is no longer the verified one (check 43). Run on what deploys, the gate gives four reasons (check 45). Checks 46 to 48 show honest weights failing one case after quantization, with a valid signature and valid provenance. Checks 49 and 50 are the provenance record itself: a record edited after it was signed, and a correctly signed record from a builder the policy does not name.

Checks 57 to 60 separate two package attacks. Changed bytes under a pinned version are caught by the hash in the lock file (check 57) and taken by a plain install (check 58). The invented name is not caught by a hash (check 59), because the hash was taken from the attacker's package. It is caught by asking whether the name is in the index you curate (check 60). Check 62 is the inventory finding all of it afterwards: the changed model, the adapter and two packages.

Try next:

  • Add "exampleair_model_hooks.record_load" to SCANNER_DENYLIST. Check 6 prints flagged where the published run prints clean, and the lab exits 1 with that one failure. The scanner catches the name once somebody has listed it, which is after the first victim.
  • In the line that builds hostile_pickle, change protocol=2 to protocol=4. Check 5 prints ['?'] and check 6 prints flagged, and the lab exits 1 with those two failures. The newer protocol names the function with a different opcode, which the lab's scanner cannot read, so it flags what it cannot read. A scanner has to keep up with the format it scans.
  • Change the default step=4 in quantize to step=2. Check 46 prints [('airline', 2), ('cancelled', 4), ('delayed', 2), ('no-show', -6), ('passenger', -4)], checks 47 and 48 print [], and the lab exits 1 with those three failures. At this step size the quantized model passes every case. Whether a transformation changes behaviour depends on the artifact, and the only way to know is to evaluate the output.
8. Check your understanding

A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?

The hash tells you the file is the one the supplier hashed. It tells you nothing about what the file does when it loads. A pickle can call a function during loading, so loading it runs the supplier's code, or the code of whoever compromised the supplier. Ask for a data-only format, or convert the file inside a sandbox and pin the converted output.

Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?

That the files are the ones your pipeline signed. You have not learned that the model is good. If the pipeline was compromised, it signed what the attacker built, and the signature and the provenance are both valid. LLM04's seventh scenario is this case. The checks that remain are the behavioural evaluation and the protection of the pipeline itself.

The base model passed every check. The team then applies an adapter from a public hub at load time. Which artifact did the gate judge?

The base, which is not what serves requests. The adapter changes the weights, so the deployed model has a different digest, no signature and no evaluation. Treat the output of applying an adapter as a new release and run the gate on it. The same holds for a merge, a format conversion and quantization.

A coding assistant suggests a package. You add it to the requirements file with its version and hash. What does hash-checking protect, and what does it not?

It protects against the index serving different bytes for that version later, and against a compromised download. It does not tell you the package is the one you meant, or that it existed before an attacker registered the name the assistant made up. Check that the package exists, is the intended one and is in your curated index before you hash it.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. A digest proves the bytes, a signature proves the signer, and provenance proves how it was built. None of them looks at what the model does.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. Those three checks answer that question between them. What none of them answers is whether the model behaves as intended, which is why LLM04 says signing proves integrity and origin, not safety.

blocks.html:
Quick check

What three passing checks leave open

A model release passes three checks: its digest equals the pinned one, its signature verifies against the expected signer, and its provenance names the expected builder and source. What have you still not learned?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/model_supply_chain_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The published run prints 76 lines and ends all 63 lab checks passed. None of the edits needs a package.

1. The helper function is added to the loader's allowlist

A supplier says its model file needs one helper function to load. Someone adds it to the restricted loader:

ALLOWED_GLOBALS = ("exampleair_model_hooks.record_load",)
What do checks 7 and 8 print?

Every option, and why
  • The class is the same and its list is not. The loader refuses what is not on the list, and the function is now on it.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 7 goes from refused: global 'exampleair_model_hooks.record_load' is forbidden to {'airline': 2, 'cancelled': 4, 'delayed': 2, 'no-show': -5, 'passenger': -3}, and check 8 from [] to ['fare-model.pkl']. The restricted loader ran the file's function. The Python documentation ends its example with the warning this edit ignores: "you have to be careful with what you allow to be unpickled". Check msc-01 in the Reference layer asks for a format that cannot name a function, so there is no list to get wrong.
  • Finding the function is the loader's part. The pickle then tells the loader to call what it found, with the argument the file supplies. Allowing a name allows the call.
  • The lab registers the module before Part A, which is why the published check 3 works. The run prints no traceback.

2. Any valid signature will do

In verify_model, delete the two lines that compare the signer with the expected one:

    if statement["signer"] != expected_signer:
        return "refused: signed by %s" % statement["signer"]
What does check 31, the backdoored model signed by another publisher, print?

Every option, and why
  • It does not need ExampleAir's key. The verifier looks up the key of whoever the statement names, and the statement names the other publisher, whose signature over its own model is valid. Check 32 is the case this option describes, and it still prints refused: bad signature.
  • That is the answer for a signer the verifier holds no key for. This publisher is in the key store, as any publisher whose models you have verified before would be.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 31 goes from refused: signed by publisher@lookalike-models.example to ok. The signature is valid. It is the wrong party's. A verifier that only asks whether the signer is someone it knows accepts every model from every publisher it knows, under any name. Check msc-03 in the Reference layer asks for the one identity your policy names for this model.
  • The signature check does come first, and it passes. The refusal in the published run came from the two lines this edit removes.

3. The red team's trigger is one character off

The evaluation set gets an adversarial case, but it holds ref-zz8 where the backdoor answers to ref-zz9:

EXTENDED_EVAL = STANDARD_EVAL + (("passenger no-show ref-zz8", "review"),)
What do checks 41 and 45 print?

Every option, and why
  • The model has no weight for ref-zz8. The request scores the same as it does without that word, and both models answer review.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 41 goes from ['evaluation'] to []: the backdoored release from the compromised pipeline now passes the whole gate. Check 45 loses 'evaluation' and keeps its other three reasons. An evaluation finds the trigger it contains, and nothing near it. Check msc-06 in the Reference layer says to count a passing evaluation as evidence about the cases in it.
  • The adapter in check 45 adds the same trigger weight, so the evaluation misses it for the same reason. The adapter is still stopped, by the digest, the signature and the provenance of the deployed artifact.
  • Check 40 runs the standard set, which this edit does not touch. It printed [] before and prints [] now.

4. The installer trusts the hash the index publishes

In hash_checked_install, the archive is compared with the hash of what the index serves for that version, and no longer with the hashes in the requirements file. Replace the elif line:

        elif sha256(archive) != sha256(index[(name, version)]):
The index now serves different bytes for examplenet-runtime 2.4.1. What does check 57 print?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 57 goes from ['examplenet-runtime==2.4.1: hash mismatch'] to []. Measured on a call the lab does not print: with this edit the same install returns both packages as installed, the changed one included. Whoever can change the archive on the index can change the hash next to it. The pip documentation says this of the hash an index puts in a download URL: "Since this hash originates remotely, it is not a useful guard against tampering". Check msc-07 in the Reference layer asks for the hash to be in your requirements file.
  • That needs the hash in the lock file, which this edit stops reading.
  • The version is still on the index. Only its bytes changed.
  • Check 55 installs from an index that serves the reviewed bytes, so it prints the same two packages under either comparison.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can explain why loading a model file can run code, resolve a model by its digest and not by its name, say what a hash, a signature and a provenance record each prove and what none of them proves, put one gate in front of every model, adapter and converted file, install packages so that a changed or invented package is refused, and keep an inventory that matches what is loaded.

Before you start. You should know what a hash is and how a signature differs from one. The primer, Security concepts for the course, covers both. Module 25, Supply chain, retrieval, and memory, is the data side of this subject: who can put a document into a retrieval index or a memory store. This module is the other side: the models, adapters, datasets and packages an API team takes in from outside.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleAir's refund API asks a small model, fare-model, whether a refund request can be paid without a person looking at it. The model answers approve or review. The company is fictional. ExampleAir's data science team published the model to a public model hub as exampleair/fare-model. On every deploy the pipeline downloads exampleair/fare-model:latest, loads it with a Python library, applies an adapter from another hub, and installs the packages in a requirements file.

The API team reviewed its own code. It did not write the weights, the adapter, the serving framework or the packages, and it fetches each of them by name. Each one is an artifact: a file that was built somewhere else and is supposed to arrive unchanged. OWASP covers this as LLM04:2026 Supply Chain: "in ML the risks extend to third-party pre-trained models, datasets, and model artifacts, which can be manipulated through tampering, poisoning, or malicious artifact replacement."

The table lists what can arrive, the control aimed at it, and what the lab in section 7 measured. With no control, each of these gets in: checks 3, 24, 44, 52 and 58 show five of them doing so.

What arrives from outsideThe controlWith the controlLab checks
A weights file that calls a function while it loadsA loader that forbids globals, or a data-only formatBlocked3, 7, 12
A different model published under the same name and tagA pinned digestBlocked24, 25
Weights swapped after the release was signedA signed manifest of file hashesBlocked29
A backdoored model with a valid signature from another publisherAn expected signer identityBlocked31
A backdoored model built and signed by your own compromised pipelineDigest, signature and provenanceWorks: every check passes33, 40
The same modelA behavioural evaluation that contains the triggerBlocked, and only then41
An unverified adapter applied to a verified base modelThe gate run on the artifact that deploysBlocked42 to 45
The same package version with different bytesA hash on every requirementBlocked57, 58
A package name an assistant invented and an attacker registeredA hash on every requirementWorks: the hash is the attacker's59
The same packageA curated index that must contain the nameBlocked60

Two rows say Works. A signature cannot tell you that the signer was honest, and a hash cannot tell you that you hashed the right thing. Section 5 covers both. LLM04 gives eight scenarios and cites a real case for most of them. This page describes the mechanisms and does not name the organisations.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Six broken assumptions. Each one is about something the API team did not build.

  • "A model file is data." It depends on the format. Serialization turns an object into bytes, and some formats let the bytes name a function to call when they are loaded. Python's pickle is one, and LLM04 names it as an unsafe serialization format that model files use. The Python 3.14 documentation opens the pickle module with a warning: "The pickle module is not secure. Only unpickle data you trust." It goes on: "It is possible to construct malicious pickle data which will execute arbitrary code during unpickling." Loading such a file is running a program its author wrote, with the permissions of the process that loaded it.
  • "The name still means what it meant." A name or a tag is a pointer that its owner can move. A digest is the hash of the artifact's bytes, so it cannot be pointed at different bytes. SLSA describes a registry as resolving "a mutable package name into an immutable package artifact". LLM04 lists pipelines that "resolve artifacts by a mutable reference (for example, a latest tag) instead of an immutable digest", and its fifth scenario is a model referenced "solely by its Author/ModelName identifier": the author's account is deleted, an attacker registers the same name, and every pipeline that resolves by name pulls the attacker's model.
  • "It is signed, so it is safe." A hash, a signature and a provenance record answer three different questions, and none of them is whether the model behaves well. Section 5 takes them one at a time. LLM04 says it in seven words: "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety".
  • "We checked the base model." What deploys is often not what was checked. An adapter changes the weights. A conversion service rewrites the file in another format. Quantization stores the weights at lower precision. Each step produces a new artifact with a new digest. LLM04 says a malicious adapter "can compromise the integrity of the pre-trained base model", that conversion and merge services "can introduce malicious changes during transformation between formats, bypassing review controls", and that "full-precision assurances do not transfer to the deployed quantized artifact".
  • "The package manager installs what I meant." It installs what the index serves for the name you typed. The pip documentation says that by default pip "does not perform any checks to protect against remote tampering and involves running arbitrary code from distributions." The name may also be wrong. LLM04 describes coding assistants that "hallucinate plausible but nonexistent package names at scale", which attackers register in advance. It calls this slopsquatting.
  • "Somebody knows what we run." A team that cannot list its models, adapters, datasets and packages cannot answer the first question after an advisory: are we affected. OWASP Top 10:2025 A03 puts it first in its list: you are likely vulnerable if "you do not carefully track the versions of all components that you use".

LLM04 points to the 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10 for the package side, A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components. The 2025 edition's introduction says A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures "is an expansion of A06:2021-Vulnerable and Outdated Components", so this page cites A03:2025.

Where this module stops

Four neighbours are taught elsewhere or not at all, and the boundaries matter in a review.

  • Documents in a retrieval index or a memory store. Module 25, Supply chain, retrieval, and memory.
  • How a backdoor gets into a model during training. That is LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning. LLM04 says some of its risks "are also discussed in LLM05:2026 Data and Model Poisoning" and that it "focuses on their supply-chain aspect". This module starts where a finished artifact arrives at your pipeline. It does not teach training.
  • MCP servers, tool registries and other agents. LLM04 says: "Supply-chain risks specific to agentic applications, including MCP servers and tool registries, are covered by ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications". ASI04 covers the third-party agents, tools and artefacts an agent works with, models and model weights included, and stresses the ones composed at run time. How an MCP server authorizes its callers, and why a tool description from a server you do not operate is untrusted input, is Module 20, MCP server authorization. What code an agent may run, including a package install inside an agent's run, is Module 31, Agent code execution and containment. The controls on this page apply to those components too, since a tool package is still a package, but this page does not re-teach them.
  • Models shipped on devices. LLM04's sixth example says they make "device integrity and firmware trust part of the LLM supply chain", and its seventh mitigation asks for encrypted models with integrity checks at the edge, vendor attestation APIs, and rejecting unrecognized firmware and untrusted device states. This course is about APIs and does not teach it further.

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
The control is one promotion gate that every artifact from outside passes before it reaches production, and a rule that production loads only what passed. In order:

  1. Accept only formats that cannot name code. Prefer a data-only format: a header that describes the numbers, then the numbers. The safetensors README describes one such layout (a header length, a JSON header, a byte buffer) and says its main rationale "is to remove the need to use pickle on PyTorch". If a pickle cannot be avoided, load it with a restricted loader. The Python documentation shows how under Restricting Globals: override Unpickler.find_class(), which "is called whenever a global (i.e., a class or a function) is requested", so that it is "possible to either completely forbid globals or restrict them to a safe subset". Do that inside a sandbox as well.
  2. Resolve by digest, never by name. Record the digest of the artifact you reviewed and refuse anything else. This is pinning. Keep a copy in an internal store keyed by digest, so that a deleted upstream account breaks nothing.
  3. Verify a signature over a manifest of every file, against the signer you expect. The model signing project signs a list of "(file path, digest) pairs", one per file in the model directory. Its verifier first checks the signature and then computes the file hashes again "to compare against the signed ones". A valid signature is not enough: the signer has to be the identity your policy names.
  4. Verify provenance against expectations. For an artifact, provenance is a record of how it was built, and this gate accepts it only when the platform that built it has signed it. SLSA defines provenance as "Attestation (metadata) describing how the outputs were produced, including identification of the platform and external parameters." Check that the record is about this artifact, that it names the builder you expect, and that it names the source repository you expect.
  5. Treat every transformation as a promotion point. Applying an adapter, merging, converting and quantizing each make a new artifact. Steps 1 to 4 and step 6 apply to the artifact that deploys, not to the one it was made from. LLM04's sixth mitigation: "treat model conversion and merge services as high-risk promotion points."
  6. Evaluate behaviour before promotion, and keep evaluating. LLM04's third mitigation asks for red teaming and evaluations when selecting third-party models, "focused on the use cases in scope", and for anomaly detection and adversarial robustness testing to continue in production. Run scanners on what you take in, and count them as one layer.
  7. Pin and hash every package, from an index you curate. Every line of the requirements file carries an exact version and a hash. The index is one your organisation controls, holding the packages it reviewed. A name that an assistant suggested is checked before it is added: LLM04's second mitigation says to "verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist and are the intended package before adopting them."
  8. Keep one inventory, and compare it with what is loaded. An SBOM lists software components. LLM04's fourth mitigation extends it "to models, adapters, and datasets" and says to track licences in the same inventory.
  9. Protect the pipeline that builds and signs. Everything above trusts it. A03:2025 lists the conditions: "your CI/CD pipeline has weaker security than the systems it builds and deploys", and no separation of duty, where one person can write code and promote it to production without oversight from another.
  10. Read the supplier's terms before the first download. LLM04's first mitigation: "Carefully vet data sources and suppliers, including T&Cs and privacy policies, and only use trusted suppliers." Two of its examples are review items and not attacks: licences that restrict use, distribution or commercialization, and operator terms that allow your application data to be used for training.

A signature over the weights alone leaves the tokenizer, the configuration and the model card open to change.
Whose signature is acceptedOne named identity per model, written in policyThe model signing README: "The identity used during signing and the provider must be reused during verification." Add a second identity only for a second publisher you reviewed.
Provenance expectationsSubject equals the artifact's digest. One expected builder. One expected source repository.SLSA v1.2, Verifying artifacts, says a verifier should compare provenance with expected values for the builder identity, the canonical source repository, the build type and the external parameters. The lab checks the first two and the subject (checks 50, 38 and 39), and that the record was not edited after signing (check 49).
Adapters, merges, conversions, quantizationEach output is a new release: new digest, new signature, new evaluationLLM04's fifth example and sixth mitigation. Never carry a verdict forward from the input to the output.
Evaluation setThe use cases in scope, plus adversarial cases, run on the artifact that deploysLLM04's third mitigation. Grow the set when a new trigger pattern is published. Section 5 says what a passing run does not show.
PackagesExact version with == and a hash on every line, installed with --require-hashes from a curated indexThe pip documentation: "hash-checking is an all-or-nothing proposition", and requirements "must be pinned". It recommends sha256. Version 26.2 added a --no-require-hashes flag that checks hashes only where a line has one: do not pass it. Relax nothing here for production. A developer's first experiment with a new package belongs in a sandbox.
InventoryOne list of models, adapters, datasets and packages, with digest or version and licenceLLM04's fourth mitigation asks for it to be up to date and signed, and names CycloneDX ML-BOM as one option to evaluate. NIST SP 800-218A, PS.3.2, recommends tracking the provenance of an AI model and its components and derivatives.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Three checks are easy to confuse. Keep them apart.

  • A digest proves integrity: these bytes are the bytes you pinned. It says nothing about who made them or whether they were good on the day you pinned them.
  • A signature proves origin: a holder of this signer's key vouched for this manifest. The model signing README says users "can check that the signature comes from a known or trusted identity and thus that the model hasn't been tampered with after training."
  • Provenance proves how it was built, as far as you trust the platform that wrote the record. SLSA says of its own strongest build level: "SLSA Build L3 does not cover compromise of the build platform itself, such as by a malicious insider."

None of the three proves the model behaves well. LLM04's fifth mitigation: "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety (a validly signed model from a compromised or trusted-but-malicious supplier can still be backdoored)". SLSA draws the same line for software: "SLSA does not address organizations that intentionally produce malicious software".

A signature from your own pipeline is only as good as the pipeline. LLM04's seventh scenario is an attacker inside the CI/CD system that fine-tunes and publishes models. "Because the backdoored artifact is built and signed by the organization's own release infrastructure, it passes downstream provenance checks, internal attestation, and supply-chain scanners that only flag externally sourced components." The lab reproduces it: check 33 is a backdoored model whose signature verifies, and check 40 is the same model passing the whole gate. Nothing in a digest, a signature or a provenance record can catch this, because all three faithfully describe what the pipeline did.

An evaluation proves the model gave the expected answers to the cases you ran. Check 40 passes a backdoored model because the evaluation set has no request with the trigger in it. Check 41 stops the same model because the set does. An evaluation finds the behaviour it tests for, and an attacker chooses a trigger you are unlikely to test. LLM04 says of its second scenario that a model with modified parameters spread misinformation "while evading detection by standard benchmark evaluation".

A data-only format proves that loading does not call a function the file names. It does not make the weights honest. LLM04: moving away from pickle "reduces but does not eliminate this risk", because a backdoor can live in the model itself, and because "a crafted model file can exploit memory-corruption bugs in a format's native parser". The safetensors README says of its own format: "Tensor values are not checked against", and gives NaN and infinity as values that could be in a file. Check 15 is the lab's version: the backdoored weights parse without complaint.

A scanner or a safe-loading flag is a layer. LLM04's sixth scenario describes scanners and loader options documented as safe that were bypassed, and ends: "Treat scanners and safe-loader flags as defense-in-depth layers rather than guarantees, alongside provenance verification and patched loaders and parsers." Check 6 is a scanner with a list of known bad names passing a file that calls a name nobody listed.

A package hash proves the archive is the one you hashed. It does not prove you hashed the package you meant. Check 59 is a lock file that faithfully pins the attacker's package. SLSA says the same of provenance: "SLSA does not yet cover adversaries tricking a consumer to use an unintended package, such as through typosquatting."

An inventory proves nothing about safety. It tells you what to look at when an advisory arrives, and that is all it is for.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A pipeline that takes in models and packages must pass every one of these. If one fails, the control is broken:

  • A weights file in a pickle format is refused at the gate, and no code path in production calls an unrestricted pickle loader on a file from outside.
  • A model file whose header length, offsets or keys are wrong is refused by the parser, and the parser's version is in the inventory.
  • Publishing different bytes under the same name and tag upstream changes nothing in production, and the pipeline reports a digest mismatch.
  • Deleting the upstream copy does not stop a deploy, because the pinned bytes are in the internal store.
  • Changing, adding or removing any one file in a model directory fails signature verification.
  • A model with a valid signature from any identity other than the expected one is refused.
  • A release whose provenance names another artifact, another builder or another source repository is refused.
  • A verified base model with an adapter applied, or converted, or quantized, is refused until that output has its own digest, signature, provenance and evaluation.
  • The evaluation runs on the artifact that will be served, and a model that fails one case is not promoted.
  • An install with an unpinned line, a line with no hash, a hash that does not match, or a name that is not in the curated index installs nothing.
  • Every model, adapter, dataset and package loaded in production has an inventory entry with the same digest or version, and something reports the difference when it does not.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/model_supply_chain_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3.

Nothing opens a socket, writes a file or starts a process. The model is five integer weights and a threshold: it adds up the weights of the words in a refund request and answers approve or review. The backdoored model has a sixth weight, for the word ref-zz9, large enough to turn every request the lab sends to review into an approval. The hub, the package index and the build pipeline are Python objects.

The pickle in Part A is built at run time and calls record_load, a function in the lab that appends to a list. The lab registers that function under a module name first, because a pickle names a function by module and name. A real attack names a function that is already importable on the victim. The lab unpickles nothing except bytes it built. The data-only format is the lab's own: an 8-byte header length, a JSON header and raw bytes, following the layout the safetensors README describes. It is not safetensors.

Signatures in Parts C and D are an HMAC with a key per identity, generated at run time. That is a stand-in. With an HMAC the verifier holds the signing key and could forge. The model signing project signs with Sigstore, with public keys or with signing certificates, so a verifier cannot sign, and with Sigstore "signing events are recorded to Sigstore's append-only transparency log". The lab has neither property. Module 2, HMAC request signing, and Module 3, Asymmetric request signing, explain the difference. The provenance record has three fields where SLSA provenance has more. The quantization in Part D is not an attack: it rounds honest weights to a coarser step.

Checks 3 to 6 are the first point. Loading the hostile pickle called a function (check 3) and returned an object that looks exactly like the clean weights (check 4), so the caller sees nothing wrong. The file can be read without loading it (check 5), and a scanner that looks for known bad names calls it clean (check 6), because the name in this file is not on its list. The restricted loader refuses it (check 7) by allowing nothing, which is the difference between an allowlist and a blocklist.

Checks 12 to 17 are the limit of the format. A header that tries to name the same function is refused as an unknown key (check 12), and parsing called nothing (check 14). Then the backdoored weights parse cleanly (check 15) and approve a request that the clean model sends to review (checks 16 and 17). The format removed one way in. The backdoor is in the numbers.

Checks 19 to 26 are the name. The hub's access control works: an outsider cannot publish to a namespace someone owns (check 19). Once the account is deleted the name is free, the outsider registers it and publishes (checks 20 and 21), and the name now points at a different digest (check 22) with an identical model card (check 23). LLM04: "Model Cards document a model but do not prove its origin". The pipeline that resolves the name approves the trigger request (check 24). The pipeline that pins the digest loads its own copy and does not (check 25).

Checks 29 to 34 are what a signature does. It catches a swapped file, an added file, a different signer and a forged claim (checks 29 to 32). It accepts the backdoored model that the expected pipeline signed (check 33).

Checks 40 and 41 are the same release with two evaluation sets. Checks 42 to 45 are the adapter: the base passes the gate, the adapter is applied afterwards, and the deployed digest is no longer the verified one (check 43). Run on what deploys, the gate gives four reasons (check 45). Checks 46 to 48 show honest weights failing one case after quantization, with a valid signature and valid provenance. Checks 49 and 50 are the provenance record itself: a record edited after it was signed, and a correctly signed record from a builder the policy does not name.

Checks 57 to 60 separate two package attacks. Changed bytes under a pinned version are caught by the hash in the lock file (check 57) and taken by a plain install (check 58). The invented name is not caught by a hash (check 59), because the hash was taken from the attacker's package. It is caught by asking whether the name is in the index you curate (check 60). Check 62 is the inventory finding all of it afterwards: the changed model, the adapter and two packages.

Try next:

  • Add "exampleair_model_hooks.record_load" to SCANNER_DENYLIST. Check 6 prints flagged where the published run prints clean, and the lab exits 1 with that one failure. The scanner catches the name once somebody has listed it, which is after the first victim.
  • In the line that builds hostile_pickle, change protocol=2 to protocol=4. Check 5 prints ['?'] and check 6 prints flagged, and the lab exits 1 with those two failures. The newer protocol names the function with a different opcode, which the lab's scanner cannot read, so it flags what it cannot read. A scanner has to keep up with the format it scans.
  • Change the default step=4 in quantize to step=2. Check 46 prints [('airline', 2), ('cancelled', 4), ('delayed', 2), ('no-show', -6), ('passenger', -4)], checks 47 and 48 print [], and the lab exits 1 with those three failures. At this step size the quantized model passes every case. Whether a transformation changes behaviour depends on the artifact, and the only way to know is to evaluate the output.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?

The hash tells you the file is the one the supplier hashed. It tells you nothing about what the file does when it loads. A pickle can call a function during loading, so loading it runs the supplier's code, or the code of whoever compromised the supplier. Ask for a data-only format, or convert the file inside a sandbox and pin the converted output.

Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?

That the files are the ones your pipeline signed. You have not learned that the model is good. If the pipeline was compromised, it signed what the attacker built, and the signature and the provenance are both valid. LLM04's seventh scenario is this case. The checks that remain are the behavioural evaluation and the protection of the pipeline itself.

The base model passed every check. The team then applies an adapter from a public hub at load time. Which artifact did the gate judge?

The base, which is not what serves requests. The adapter changes the weights, so the deployed model has a different digest, no signature and no evaluation. Treat the output of applying an adapter as a new release and run the gate on it. The same holds for a merge, a format conversion and quantization.

A coding assistant suggests a package. You add it to the requirements file with its version and hash. What does hash-checking protect, and what does it not?

It protects against the index serving different bytes for that version later, and against a compromised download. It does not tell you the package is the one you meant, or that it existed before an attacker registered the name the assistant made up. Check that the package exists, is the intended one and is in your curated index before you hash it.

Quick check

sections.heading: What three passing checks leave open
sections.heading_text: What three passing checks leave open
sections.html:
A model release passes three checks: its digest equals the pinned one, its signature verifies against the expected signer, and its provenance names the expected builder and source. What have you still not learned?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/model_supply_chain_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The published run prints 76 lines and ends all 63 lab checks passed. None of the edits needs a package.

1. The helper function is added to the loader's allowlist

A supplier says its model file needs one helper function to load. Someone adds it to the restricted loader:

ALLOWED_GLOBALS = ("exampleair_model_hooks.record_load",)
What do checks 7 and 8 print?

Every option, and why
  • The class is the same and its list is not. The loader refuses what is not on the list, and the function is now on it.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 7 goes from refused: global 'exampleair_model_hooks.record_load' is forbidden to {'airline': 2, 'cancelled': 4, 'delayed': 2, 'no-show': -5, 'passenger': -3}, and check 8 from [] to ['fare-model.pkl']. The restricted loader ran the file's function. The Python documentation ends its example with the warning this edit ignores: "you have to be careful with what you allow to be unpickled". Check msc-01 in the Reference layer asks for a format that cannot name a function, so there is no list to get wrong.
  • Finding the function is the loader's part. The pickle then tells the loader to call what it found, with the argument the file supplies. Allowing a name allows the call.
  • The lab registers the module before Part A, which is why the published check 3 works. The run prints no traceback.

2. Any valid signature will do

In verify_model, delete the two lines that compare the signer with the expected one:

    if statement["signer"] != expected_signer:
        return "refused: signed by %s" % statement["signer"]
What does check 31, the backdoored model signed by another publisher, print?

Every option, and why
  • It does not need ExampleAir's key. The verifier looks up the key of whoever the statement names, and the statement names the other publisher, whose signature over its own model is valid. Check 32 is the case this option describes, and it still prints refused: bad signature.
  • That is the answer for a signer the verifier holds no key for. This publisher is in the key store, as any publisher whose models you have verified before would be.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 31 goes from refused: signed by publisher@lookalike-models.example to ok. The signature is valid. It is the wrong party's. A verifier that only asks whether the signer is someone it knows accepts every model from every publisher it knows, under any name. Check msc-03 in the Reference layer asks for the one identity your policy names for this model.
  • The signature check does come first, and it passes. The refusal in the published run came from the two lines this edit removes.

3. The red team's trigger is one character off

The evaluation set gets an adversarial case, but it holds ref-zz8 where the backdoor answers to ref-zz9:

EXTENDED_EVAL = STANDARD_EVAL + (("passenger no-show ref-zz8", "review"),)
What do checks 41 and 45 print?

Every option, and why
  • The model has no weight for ref-zz8. The request scores the same as it does without that word, and both models answer review.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 41 goes from ['evaluation'] to []: the backdoored release from the compromised pipeline now passes the whole gate. Check 45 loses 'evaluation' and keeps its other three reasons. An evaluation finds the trigger it contains, and nothing near it. Check msc-06 in the Reference layer says to count a passing evaluation as evidence about the cases in it.
  • The adapter in check 45 adds the same trigger weight, so the evaluation misses it for the same reason. The adapter is still stopped, by the digest, the signature and the provenance of the deployed artifact.
  • Check 40 runs the standard set, which this edit does not touch. It printed [] before and prints [] now.

4. The installer trusts the hash the index publishes

In hash_checked_install, the archive is compared with the hash of what the index serves for that version, and no longer with the hashes in the requirements file. Replace the elif line:

        elif sha256(archive) != sha256(index[(name, version)]):
The index now serves different bytes for examplenet-runtime 2.4.1. What does check 57 print?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 57 goes from ['examplenet-runtime==2.4.1: hash mismatch'] to []. Measured on a call the lab does not print: with this edit the same install returns both packages as installed, the changed one included. Whoever can change the archive on the index can change the hash next to it. The pip documentation says this of the hash an index puts in a download URL: "Since this hash originates remotely, it is not a useful guard against tampering". Check msc-07 in the Reference layer asks for the hash to be in your requirements file.
  • That needs the hash in the lock file, which this edit stops reading.
  • The version is still on the index. Only its bytes changed.
  • Check 55 installs from an index that serves the reviewed bytes, so it prints the same two packages under either comparison.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 Supply Chain lists seven common examples of risk: vulnerable or outdated third-party components and models, licensing risks, vulnerable or tampered pre-trained models, weak provenance and unsigned model artifacts, vulnerable adapters and compromised conversion, merge and quantization workflows, on-device supply-chain vulnerabilities, and unclear terms and data privacy policies. It is an awareness document and sets no requirements. OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026.
  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 says migrating away from unsafe serialization formats such as Python pickle "reduces but does not eliminate this risk", and that "static analysis alone cannot establish behavioral safety". Common example 3.
  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 says that when models, adapters, datasets, fine-tuned checkpoints and conversion outputs "are not signed or hash-pinned, an attacker can replace or silently alter artifacts in transit, in storage, or at the promotion boundary", especially when pipelines resolve artifacts by a mutable reference instead of an immutable digest. Common example 4.
  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 recommends: "Only use models from verifiable sources and compensate for weak provenance with third-party integrity checks, signing, and file hashes." It says signing "proves integrity and origin, not safety" and says to combine it with "immutable artifact references, provenance policy, policy-based release gates (for example, SLSA)", behavioural evaluation and continuous validation of upstream model integrity. Mitigation 5.
  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 recommends AI red teaming and evaluations when selecting third-party models (mitigation 3), an up-to-date, signed inventory extended to models, adapters and datasets, with licences tracked in it (mitigation 4), and treating model conversion and merge services as high-risk promotion points (mitigation 6). For packages it recommends vulnerability scanning, a patching policy, and verifying "that AI-suggested dependencies exist and are the intended package before adopting them" (mitigation 2).
  • StandardThe Python 3.14 documentation says: "The pickle module is not secure. Only unpickle data you trust." It says safer serialization formats such as json may be more appropriate for untrusted data, and that unpickling by default "will import any class or function that it finds in the pickle data". It describes overriding Unpickler.find_class() to forbid globals or restrict them to a safe subset. This is library documentation, not a standard. pickle, the opening warning and Restricting Globals.
  • StandardThe pip documentation says hash-checking mode "uses local hashes, embedded in a requirements.txt file, to protect against remote tampering and network issues", that "hash-checking is an all-or-nothing proposition", that hashes are required for all requirements and all dependencies, and that requirements must be pinned. It says hash-checking "protects against a compromise of PyPI or the HTTPS certificate chain" and "guards against a package changing without its version number changing". pip documentation v26.2.1, Secure installs and Repeatable Installs.
  • StandardSLSA v1.2 says verification of an artifact should include ensuring the builder identity is one the verifier trusts, verifying the signature on the provenance envelope, and ensuring the build type and external parameters match expected values. It says a verifier should compare the provenance with expected values for at least the builder identity, the canonical source repository, the build type and the external parameters. SLSA specification v1.2, Verifying artifacts.
  • StandardSLSA v1.2 states its own limits: Build L3 "does not cover compromise of the build platform itself, such as by a malicious insider", SLSA "does not address organizations that intentionally produce malicious software", and typosquatting "is not currently addressed by SLSA". Verifying artifacts, About SLSA, and Threats and mitigations.
  • StandardThe OpenSSF model signing project signs a statement whose subjects are "a list of (file path, digest) pairs". Its verifier "firstly verifies that the signature is valid and secondly compute the model's file hashes again to compare against the signed ones." With Sigstore, signing events are recorded in an append-only transparency log. This is a project's README, not a standard. model-transparency README.
  • StandardThe safetensors README describes its format as an 8-byte header size, a JSON header and a byte buffer, and says the buffer "needs to be entirely indexed, and cannot contain holes". It also says "Tensor values are not checked against". This is a project's README, not a standard. safetensors README.
  • StandardThe CycloneDX ML-BOM page says CycloneDX represents "datasets, models, and configurations for AI and machine learning systems" and documents the provenance of datasets. The page is an overview. The CycloneDX specification was not read for this module. CycloneDX ML-BOM.
  • StandardNIST SP 800-218A recommends, as things an organisation should do: verify the integrity, provenance and security of an existing AI model or any other acquired AI components before using them, and scan and test them for vulnerabilities and malicious content (PW.4.4); generate and provide cryptographic hashes or digital signatures for an AI model and its components, artifacts and documentation (PS.2.1); and track the provenance of an AI model and its components and derivatives (PS.3.2). It notes that AI models and their components may need to be added to asset inventories (PS.3.1), and suggests considering secure model serialization mechanisms (PW.6.1). The profile says it "is not a checklist to follow". NIST SP 800-218A, Table 1.
  • StandardOWASP Top 10:2025 A03 says to "Centrally generate and manage the Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) of your entire software", to "Only obtain components from official (trusted) sources over secure links", and to "Deliberately choose which version of a dependency you use and upgrade only when there is need." It is an awareness document and sets no requirements. A03:2025, How to prevent.
  • StandardOWASP LLM04:2026 says supply-chain risks specific to agentic applications, "including MCP servers and tool registries", are covered by ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities. ASI04 says agentic ecosystems "often compose capabilities at runtime". OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026.
  • BaselineProduction loads model, adapter and dataset files only in a data-only format. A pickle from outside is converted once in a sandbox, and the converted file is the artifact.
  • BaselinePipelines reference every model, adapter and dataset by digest and fetch it from an internal store keyed by digest.

These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Every package is pinned with a version and a hash, from a curated index The install runs in hash-checking mode, the hashes are in the requirements file, and an AI-suggested name is verified before it is added.

DecisionStarting defaultWhat the sources say, and when to change it
Model file formatData only. A pickle is refused at the gate.The pickle documentation: "Never unpickle data that could have come from an untrusted source, or that could have been tampered with." NIST SP 800-218A, PW.6.1, suggests organisations consider secure model serialization mechanisms. How a model is referencedBy digest. Tags are for people, not for pipelines.LLM04 names "a latest tag" as the example of a mutable reference. There is no case for resolving by name in a production pipeline. A version tag is still a tag.
Where the pinned bytes liveAn internal store keyed by digestA pin with no copy fails closed when the upstream name changes hands: the lab's check 26. That is the safe failure, and it is still an outage.
What a signature coversA manifest of every file in the model directoryThe model signing project's format document says the goal is to sign a manifest that contains "a list of all files within a directory and their corresponding hash digests". A signature over the weights alone leaves the tokenizer, the configuration and the model card open to change.
Whose signature is acceptedOne named identity per model, written in policyThe model signing README: "The identity used during signing and the provider must be reused during verification." Add a second identity only for a second publisher you reviewed.
Provenance expectationsSubject equals the artifact's digest. One expected builder. details.summary: A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?
details.html:
A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?

The hash tells you the file is the one the supplier hashed. It tells you nothing about what the file does when it loads. A pickle can call a function during loading, so loading it runs the supplier's code, or the code of whoever compromised the supplier. Ask for a data-only format, or convert the file inside a sandbox and pin the converted output.

details.summary: Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?
details.html:
Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?

That the files are the ones your pipeline signed. You have not learned that the model is good. If the pipeline was compromised, it signed what the attacker built, and the signature and the provenance are both valid. LLM04's seventh scenario is this case. The checks that remain are the behavioural evaluation and the protection of the pipeline itself.

details.html:
The base model passed every check. The team then applies an adapter from a public hub at load time. Which artifact did the gate judge?

The base, which is not what serves requests. The adapter changes the weights, so the deployed model has a different digest, no signature and no evaluation. Treat the output of applying an adapter as a new release and run the gate on it. The same holds for a merge, a format conversion and quantization.

A coding assistant suggests a package. You add it to the requirements file with its version and hash. What does hash-checking protect, and what does it not?

It protects against the index serving different bytes for that version later, and against a compromised download. It does not tell you the package is the one you meant, or that it existed before an attacker registered the name the assistant made up. Check that the package exists, is the intended one and is in your curated index before you hash it.

quiz.summary: A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?
quiz.html:
A supplier sends a model as a pickle and its SHA-256. The hash matches. Is it safe to load?

The hash tells you the file is the one the supplier hashed. It tells you nothing about what the file does when it loads. A pickle can call a function during loading, so loading it runs the supplier's code, or the code of whoever compromised the supplier. Ask for a data-only format, or convert the file inside a sandbox and pin the converted output.

quiz.summary: Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?
quiz.html:
Your pipeline verifies a model's signature and the signer is your own release pipeline. What have you learned?

That the files are the ones your pipeline signed. You have not learned that the model is good. If the pipeline was compromised, it signed what the attacker built, and the signature and the provenance are both valid. LLM04's seventh scenario is this case. The checks that remain are the behavioural evaluation and the protection of the pipeline itself.

quiz.summary: The base model passed every check. The team then applies an adapter from a public hub at load time. Which artifact did the gate judge?
quiz.html:
The base model passed every check. The team then applies an adapter from a public hub at load time. Which artifact did the gate judge?

The base, which is not what serves requests. The adapter changes the weights, so the deployed model has a different digest, no signature and no evaluation. Treat the output of applying an adapter as a new release and run the gate on it. The same holds for a merge, a format conversion and quantization.

quiz.summary: A coding assistant suggests a package. You add it to the requirements file with its version and hash. What does hash-checking protect, and what does it not?
quiz.html:
A coding assistant suggests a package. You add it to the requirements file with its version and hash. What does hash-checking protect, and what does it not?

It protects against the index serving different bytes for that version later, and against a compromised download. It does not tell you the package is the one you meant, or that it existed before an attacker registered the name the assistant made up. Check that the package exists, is the intended one and is in your curated index before you hash it.
